claim: After an initial period of steady elongation driven by the actomyosin network, muscle contractions operate a quasi-periodic sequence of bending, rotation, and torsion in C. elegans embryos.
source: As demonstrated experimentally, after an initial period of steady elongation driven by the actomyosin network, muscle contractions operate a quasi-periodic sequence of bending, rotation, and torsion, that leads to the final fourfold size of the embryos before hatching.
evidence: The claim is stated as being demonstrated experimentally, indicating empirical support.

claim: C. elegans embryos reach a final fourfold size before hatching.
source: As demonstrated experimentally, after an initial period of steady elongation driven by the actomyosin network, muscle contractions operate a quasi-periodic sequence of bending, rotation, and torsion, that leads to the final fourfold size of the embryos before hatching.
evidence: The claim is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Mechanical stresses play a critical role during embryogenesis.
source: Mechanical stresses play a critical role during embryogenesis, affecting complex biological tissues such as the skin, the brain, and the interior of organs (Goriely, 2017).

claim: The pattern of the intestine has been interpreted as the result of compressive stresses generated by growth.
source: There are many studies in recent decades, for example, the pattern of the intestine (Coulombre and Coulombre, 1958; Hannezo et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Ben Amar and Jia, 2013; Shyer et al., 2013), the brain cortex (Toro and Burnod, 2005; Goriely et al., 2015; Ben Amar and Bordner, 2017; Tallinen et al., 2016), and the circumvolutions of the fingerprints (Kücken and Newell, 2005; Ciarletta and Ben Amar, 2012), which have been interpreted as the result of compressive stresses generated by the growth that occurs a few months after fertilization in humans.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Myosin II is the most abundant molecular motor during epithelial cell morphogenesis.
source: For example, independent of growth, stresses can be generated by different molecular motors, among which myosin II, linked to actin filaments, is the most abundant during epithelial cell morphogenesis (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009) and cell motility (Cowan and Hyman, 2007; Olson and Sahai, 2009; Palumbo et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009.

claim: Myosin II is linked to actin filaments.
source: For example, independent of growth, stresses can be generated by different molecular motors, among which myosin II, linked to actin filaments, is the most abundant during epithelial cell morphogenesis (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009) and cell motility (Cowan and Hyman, 2007; Olson and Sahai, 2009; Palumbo et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Spatial distribution and dynamics of myosin II strongly influence the morphogenetic process.
source: Spatial distribution and dynamics of myosin II strongly influence the morphogenetic process (Levayer and Lecuit, 2012; Lv et al., 2022), as demonstrated for Drosophila (Bertet et al., 2004; Blankenship et al., 2006; Saxena et al., 2014; Shindo and Wallingford, 2014) and also for C. elegans embryos (Priess and Hirsh, 1986; Gally et al., 2009; Ben Amar et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Embryonic elongation of C. elegans before hatching occurs in the absence of growth.
source: Embryonic elongation of C. elegans before hatching provides an attractive model of matter reorganization in the absence of growth.
evidence: The claim is stated as a characteristic of the C. elegans model system.

claim: C. elegans embryonic elongation occurs after ventral enclosure and takes about 240 min.
source: It occurs after ventral enclosure and takes about 240 min to transform the lima bean-shaped embryo into the final elongated worm form: the embryo elongates four times along the anterior/posterior axis by McKeown et al., 1998.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McKeown et al., 1998.

claim: The C. elegans embryo elongates four times along the anterior/posterior axis.
source: It occurs after ventral enclosure and takes about 240 min to transform the lima bean-shaped embryo into the final elongated worm form: the embryo elongates four times along the anterior/posterior axis by McKeown et al., 1998.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McKeown et al., 1998.

claim: In C. elegans embryonic development, there is no cell migration, cell division, or significant change in embryonic volume during the post-enclosure period.
source: However, in contrast to Drosophila and zebrafish embryonic development, there is no cell migration, cell division, or significant change in embryonic volume (Sulston et al., 1983; Priess and Hirsh, 1986), only remarkable epidermal elongation drives the entire morphogenetic process of C. elegans in the post-enclosure period.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sulston et al., 1983 and Priess and Hirsh, 1986.

claim: Epidermal elongation drives the entire morphogenetic process of C. elegans in the post-enclosure period.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sulston et al., 1983 and Priess and Hirsh, 1986.

claim: There are two experimentally identified driving forces for C. elegans elongation: actomyosin contractility in seam cells and muscle activity beneath the epidermis.
source: There are two experimentally identified driving forces for the elongation: the actomyosin contractility in the seam cells of the epidermis, which appear to persist throughout the whole elongation process, and the muscle activity beneath the epidermis, which begins after the 1.7∼1.8-fold stage.
evidence: The claim is stated as experimentally identified.

claim: Actomyosin contractility in seam cells persists throughout the whole elongation process.
source: There are two experimentally identified driving forces for the elongation: the actomyosin contractility in the seam cells of the epidermis, which appear to persist throughout the whole elongation process, and the muscle activity beneath the epidermis, which begins after the 1.7∼1.8-fold stage.

claim: Muscle activity beneath the epidermis begins after the 1.7∼1.8-fold stage.

claim: The elongation process of C. elegans can be divided into two stages: early elongation and late elongation, depending on muscle activation.
source: Consequently, the elongation process of C. elegans could be divided into two stages: the early elongation and the late elongation, depending on the muscle activation, and Figure 1A shows the whole elongation process (Vuong-Brender et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and citation to Vuong-Brender et al., 2017a.

claim: A model including pre-stress, active compressive ortho-radial stress, and passive stress quantitatively predicts early elongation up to ~70% of the initial length.
source: Based on the geometry of a hollow cylinder composed of dorsal, ventral, and seam cells, a model including the pre-stress responsible for the enclosure, the active compressive ortho-radial stress combined with the passive stress quantitatively predicts the elongation, but only up to ∼70% of the initial length.
evidence: The claim is based on a previously developed model.

claim: The actomyosin network and muscles together drive the full elongation during the late elongation phase.
source: For the late elongation phase, the actomyosin network and the muscles together drive the full elongation during this phase (Vuong-Brender et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vuong-Brender et al., 2017a.

claim: Mutants with muscle defects are unable to complete the elongation process, even though the actomyosin network functions normally.
source: The muscles play an important role and mutants with muscle defects are unable to complete the elongation process, even though the actomyosin network functions normally (Lardennois et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lardennois et al., 2019.

claim: C. elegans has four rows of muscles, two under the dorsal epidermis and two under the ventral epidermis.
source: Figure 1B shows a schematic image of the C. elegans body (Zhang et al., 2011) with four rows of muscles, two of which are under the dorsal epidermis and the other two are under the ventral epidermis.

claim: C. elegans exhibits systematic rotations accompanying each contraction.
